tokens.heading: ABSTRACT
tokens.text:
The increasing adoption of Outcome-Based Education (OBE), accreditation frameworks, and
digital learning environments has significantly increased the volume of academic documents
requiring evaluation, including internship reports, project reports, and technical submissions.
Traditional assessment practices rely heavily on manual review, making the evaluation process
time-consuming, subjective, and difficult to scale while maintaining consistency across large
student cohorts. Although recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Natural Language
Processing (NLP) have enabled automated content analysis and feedback generation, existing
approaches primarily focus on textual quality or generic document evaluation and often lack
curriculum awareness, educational context, and explainable assessment mechanisms. This project
presents Digi Assessor: Griffin Model 1.0, a Semantic Learning Alignment Model designed to
automate curriculum-aware assessment of internship and academic reports. The proposed
framework integrates curriculum intelligence generation, semantic topic extraction, curriculum
mapping, semantic similarity analysis, significance assessment, format compliance evaluation, and
bulk assessment capabilities within a unified assessment pipeline. Curriculum documents are
transformed into structured knowledge representations and semantically aligned with report
content using transformer-based embedding models, enabling the evaluation of curriculum
coverage and learning relevance beyond traditional keyword-matching techniques. A machine
learning-based significance assessment module estimates the technical contribution and
educational value of report content, while automated processing supports consistent evaluation
across multiple reports with reduced assessment effort. The framework was implemented using
modern NLP and machine learning technologies and evaluated on internship reports from the B.Sc.
Data Science program at GSFC University. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of
the proposed approach in performing curriculum-aware document assessment, identifying
curriculum alignment, generating explainable evaluation outcomes, and supporting scalable
academic assessment. The proposed model contributes toward the development of intelligent
educational assessment systems that improve evaluation consistency, reduce faculty workload, and
strengthen curriculum-driven quality assurance practices.

tokens.heading: 1.1 Background and Motivation
tokens.text:
The increasing adoption of digital learning platforms, Outcome-Based Education (OBE)
frameworks, and accreditation-driven academic processes has significantly increased the volume
of educational documents generated within higher education institutions. Internship reports,
project reports, curriculum documents, and assessment records play a critical role in measuring
student achievement, program effectiveness, and institutional quality assurance.
Traditionally, these documents are evaluated manually by faculty members. Although manual
assessment enables expert judgment, it is often time-consuming, resource-intensive, and prone to
inconsistencies among evaluators. As student enrolments and document volumes continue to grow,
maintaining assessment quality and consistency becomes increasingly challenging. Recent studies
highlight the growing role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in educational assessment and evaluation,
demonstrating its potential to improve efficiency, reduce workload, and support evidence-based
academic decision making [1], [2], [3]However, the integration of AI into assessment processes
introduces new challenges related to reliability, transparency, and contextual understanding.
Internship report assessment represents a particularly complex task because evaluators must
simultaneously assess document structure, curriculum relevance, topic coverage, learning
outcomes, technical quality, and educational significance. Such multidimensional evaluation
requires considerable expertise and effort, motivating the need for intelligent automated
assessment systems capable of supporting educational institutions.

tokens.heading: 1.2 Problem Statement
tokens.text:
Recent advancements in Generative Artificial Intelligence and Large Language Models (LLMs)
have enabled automated feedback generation, content evaluation, and scoring of educational
documents. Systems such as ChatGPT, Gemini, and other AI-assisted educational tools can
analyze textual content and generate assessment-related outputs with considerable accuracy [2],
[4].
However, existing AI-based assessment systems often lack curriculum awareness, explainability,
institutional customization, and consistent evaluation mechanisms. Most systems primarily focus
on linguistic quality or content generation rather than assessing curriculum alignment, educational

significance, and learning outcome attainment. Consequently, educational institutions still face
difficulties in adopting AI-based assessment systems for reliable academic evaluation.
Therefore, there is a need for a curriculum-aware assessment framework capable of integrating
document analysis, curriculum mapping, semantic understanding, and explainable evaluation
within a unified system.

tokens.heading: 1.3 Existing Solutions
tokens.text: Several approaches have been adopted for educational assessment and curriculum evaluation.

tokens.heading: Manual Faculty Assessment
tokens.text:
The most widely used approach remains manual assessment conducted by faculty members. This
method benefits from human expertise and contextual understanding but suffers from scalability,
consistency, and time-efficiency limitations.

tokens.heading: Generative AI Systems
tokens.text:
Modern generative AI systems such as ChatGPT and Gemini are capable of generating feedback,
summaries, evaluations, and recommendations. These systems leverage large-scale language
models to process educational content and provide automated responses [1], [2], [3]

tokens.heading: Curriculum Mapping Systems
tokens.text:
Curriculum mapping tools are widely used to establish relationships between Course Learning
Outcomes (CLOs) and Program Learning Outcomes (PLOs). These systems support accreditation,
quality assurance, and curriculum review activities [5], [6], [7]

tokens.heading: NLP-Based Educational Assessment Systems
tokens.text:
Recent research has introduced Natural Language Processing (NLP) approaches for automated
grading, curriculum mapping, and educational evaluation. NLP-based systems can identify
semantic relationships, evaluate content relevance, and improve assessment efficiency while
reducing manual effort [8], [9].
Semantic Similarity Systems

tokens.text:
To address the identified limitations, this project proposes Digi Assessor – Griffin Model 1.0, an
intelligent educational document assessment framework designed specifically for curriculum-
aware internship report evaluation.
The proposed framework integrates multiple assessment components within a unified architecture:
1.
Curriculum Mapping Engine
2.
Topic Extraction Module
3.
Semantic Similarity Analysis
4.
Curriculum Coverage Assessment
5.
Multi-Factor Evaluation Framework
6.
Explainable Feedback Generation
7.
Significance Testing Mechanism
Unlike conventional assessment systems, Griffin Model 1.0 evaluates both document quality and
educational relevance, enabling curriculum-aware and explainable assessment of internship and
academic reports. The framework combines curriculum intelligence, semantic analysis, and
educational significance evaluation within a single automated pipeline.

tokens.heading: 1.6 Research Gap
tokens.text:
Existing educational assessment systems primarily focus on isolated tasks such as rubric-based
grading, content evaluation, feedback generation, curriculum mapping, or semantic similarity
analysis. Research efforts have successfully automated CLO-PLO alignment, semantic grading,
and curriculum analysis using rule-based and NLP-based approaches [5], [6], [8], [9]
However, limited research exists on an integrated assessment framework capable of
simultaneously performing curriculum mapping, topic extraction, semantic similarity analysis,
curriculum coverage assessment, significance testing, and explainable scoring. Current systems
generally address only a subset of these functionalities and do not provide a comprehensive
educational document intelligence framework.

and rarely incorporate educational significance evaluation within the assessment workflow [10],

tokens.heading: 2.1 Introduction
tokens.text:
The increasing adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Natural Language Processing (NLP), and
data-driven educational technologies has transformed the field of academic assessment.
Educational institutions are increasingly seeking automated solutions capable of improving
assessment efficiency, consistency, and scalability while maintaining educational quality. Recent
research has explored AI-assisted grading, curriculum mapping, semantic similarity analysis, and
automated feedback generation as mechanisms to support educational evaluation processes.
This chapter reviews the existing literature related to AI-based assessment systems, curriculum
mapping methodologies, semantic similarity techniques, and NLP-driven educational evaluation
frameworks. The reviewed studies provide the theoretical and technical foundation for the
development of Digi Assessor – Griffin Model 1.0.

tokens.heading: 2.2 Artificial Intelligence in Educational Assessment
tokens.text:
Artificial Intelligence has emerged as a significant technological advancement in educational
assessment and evaluation. Recent studies indicate that AI technologies can support automated
grading, assessment analytics, adaptive feedback generation, and educational decision-making
processes .[1]
Tanberkan et al. [1] reported that AI-driven assessment systems can improve evaluation
consistency, reduce faculty workload, and enhance educational quality assurance processes.
Similarly, Karadag [2] highlighted the growing role of AI in online assessment environments,
emphasizing its ability to automate evaluation activities while improving scalability and
accessibility.
A systematic review conducted by González-Calatayud et al. [3] examined the application of AI
in student assessment and concluded that AI-based systems are increasingly used for formative
evaluation, automatic grading, and educational analytics. However, the study also identified
concerns related to explainability, pedagogical transparency, and educational interpretation.
Recent advancements in Generative AI have further expanded assessment capabilities. Mekheimer
[4] demonstrated that AI-assisted feedback systems can improve writing quality and learner
performance through iterative feedback generation. Despite these benefits, most existing AI-based

tokens.heading: 2.2 Artificial Intelligence in Educational Assessment
tokens.text:
9
assessment systems focus primarily on textual quality and feedback generation rather than
curriculum-aware evaluation.
These findings suggest that AI possesses significant potential for educational assessment but
requires stronger integration with curriculum intelligence and explainable evaluation mechanisms.

tokens.heading: 2.3 Curriculum Mapping and Outcome-Based Education
tokens.text:
Outcome-Based Education (OBE) emphasizes the alignment of educational activities,
assessments, and learning outcomes. Curriculum mapping serves as a fundamental process for
establishing relationships between Course Learning Outcomes (CLOs), Program Learning
Outcomes (PLOs), and educational objectives.
Alshanqiti et al. [5] proposed a rule-based framework for automating curriculum mapping
activities. Their study demonstrated the feasibility of reducing manual effort while maintaining
mapping accuracy through structured rule-based approaches.
Zaki et al. [6]  further extended curriculum mapping research through Natural Language
Processing techniques capable of automatically identifying semantic relationships between CLOs
and PLOs. Their findings indicate that NLP-based curriculum mapping can significantly improve
educational program evaluation and accreditation support.
More recently, Quince [7] investigated the use of Generative AI for scalable curriculum mapping
and compared AI-generated mappings with human expert evaluations. The study revealed
promising results while emphasizing the continued importance of contextual interpretation and
human validation.
Although these studies demonstrate substantial progress in curriculum mapping automation, most
existing approaches focus primarily on learning outcome alignment and do not evaluate curriculum
coverage within student-generated academic documents.

tokens.heading: 2.4 Semantic Similarity and NLP-Based Assessment
tokens.text:
Semantic similarity represents one of the most important concepts in Natural Language Processing
and educational document analysis. Semantic similarity techniques attempt to determine the
degree of conceptual similarity between textual entities beyond simple keyword matching.

tokens.heading: 2.4 Semantic Similarity and NLP-Based Assessment
tokens.text:
10
Early research by Miller and Charles [13] established foundational principles for measuring
semantic relationships between linguistic concepts. Subsequently, Kandola et al. [12] introduced
machine learning approaches for semantic similarity estimation, demonstrating improved
contextual understanding compared to traditional methods.
Chandrasekaran and Mago [11] presented a comprehensive survey of semantic similarity
techniques and highlighted the evolution from lexical approaches toward embedding-based and
transformer-based methods. Their findings indicate that modern semantic representations
significantly improve contextual understanding and semantic interpretation.
Recent advancements in embedding technologies have further enhanced semantic analysis
capabilities. Szymanski et al. [10]  demonstrated that improved word embedding architectures can
significantly strengthen semantic alignment performance across NLP applications.
Chandrasekaran and Mago [14] conducted a comparative analysis of word embedding techniques
for semantic similarity assessment and reported that contextual language models outperform
traditional embedding approaches, particularly for complex textual content.
These developments have enabled the use of semantic similarity techniques in educational
assessment, curriculum mapping, automated grading, and document evaluation systems.

tokens.section: 2.5 Existing Assessment Systems and Research Gap Analysis
tokens.heading: 2.5 Existing Assessment Systems and Research Gap Analysis
tokens.text:
Numerous studies have explored automated grading and AI-assisted educational evaluation.
Ayaan and Ng [8] proposed an automated grading framework utilizing Natural Language
Processing and semantic analysis to evaluate student responses. Their results demonstrated the
effectiveness of semantic evaluation techniques in assessment automation.
Similarly, Agrawal et al.  [9] introduced a comprehensive NLP and deep learning-based
assessment framework capable of evaluating subjective responses through multiple assessment
dimensions. Their approach improved grading consistency and reduced evaluator dependency.
While existing assessment systems have successfully incorporated semantic analysis, automated
grading, curriculum mapping, and AI-generated feedback, these capabilities are generally
implemented as isolated components. Current systems rarely integrate curriculum intelligence
generation, curriculum mapping, semantic similarity analysis, curriculum coverage assessment,

This research gap forms the primary motivation behind the development of Digi Assessor – Griffin

tokens.text:
Digi Assessor: Griffin Model 1.0 is a curriculum-aware academic assessment framework developed to
automate the evaluation of internship and academic reports through semantic analysis, curriculum mapping,
significance assessment, and format compliance verification. The framework integrates Natural Language
Processing (NLP), machine learning, and semantic similarity techniques to assess curriculum alignment,
topic relevance, and educational significance while generating explainable assessment outcomes. This
chapter presents the overall system architecture, core modules, mathematical formulations, assessment
methodology, and algorithmic workflow adopted in the proposed framework
.

tokens.heading: 3.6 Bloom's Taxonomy Evaluation
tokens.text:
Bloom's Taxonomy provides a hierarchical framework for evaluating cognitive learning outcomes
and educational achievement. Since internship reports often demonstrate varying levels of
knowledge acquisition and practical application, Griffin Model 1.0 incorporates Bloom's
Taxonomy evaluation to estimate the cognitive depth reflected within report content.
The proposed framework analyzes extracted report concepts and textual descriptions to identify
evidence of learning activities corresponding to Bloom's six cognitive levels: Remember,
Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, and Create. By examining contextual indicators, action
verbs, technical explanations, implementation details, and problem-solving approaches, the system
estimates the cognitive complexity demonstrated by a student throughout the internship report.

tokens.heading: 4.1 Introduction
tokens.text:
Following the design and development of Digi Assessor – Griffin Model 1.0, the proposed
framework was implemented and evaluated using internship reports from the B.Sc. Data Science
curriculum. The primary objective of the implementation phase was to validate the capability of
the proposed system in performing curriculum-aware assessment through semantic analysis,
curriculum mapping, significance evaluation, and automated report assessment. This chapter
presents the implementation process, experimental observations, and assessment outcomes
obtained from the developed framework.

tokens.heading: 4.2 System Implementation
tokens.text:
Digi Assessor – Griffin Model 1.0 was implemented as a web-based assessment platform using
Python and Flask. The system integrates curriculum intelligence generation, topic extraction,
semantic similarity analysis, curriculum mapping, significance prediction, and report generation
into a unified workflow.
The implementation process begins with curriculum ingestion, where curriculum documents are
transformed into structured curriculum intelligence repositories. Internship reports are
subsequently processed through document parsing and semantic analysis modules, enabling the
identification of curriculum-relevant concepts and educational outcomes.

tokens.heading: 4.3 Bulk Assessment and Parallel Execution
tokens.text:
One of the primary objectives of Griffin Model 1.0 is to support scalable academic assessment
through automated processing of multiple reports. Unlike conventional assessment approaches that
evaluate reports individually, the proposed framework incorporates batch processing mechanisms
that enable simultaneous assessment of large document collections while maintaining evaluation
consistency. To evaluate scalability, experiments were conducted using different assessment
workloads, including single-report assessment, medium-scale batch assessment, and large-scale
batch assessment. The processing time required for each workload was recorded and analyzed
The experimental results indicate that Griffin Model 1.0 maintains efficient processing
performance as workload size increases. While the assessment of a single report required
approximately 1.5 minutes, batch assessment of 25 reports required an average of only 0.60
minutes per report. Similarly, during the evaluation of 48 reports, the average processing time
further decreased to approximately 0.54 minutes per report.

tokens.heading: 4.3 Bulk Assessment and Parallel Execution

These observations demonstrate that the framework benefits from parallelized processing and
shared computational operations performed during curriculum loading, semantic embedding
generation, and assessment execution. As workload size increases, the computational overhead
associated with initialization and resource allocation is distributed across a larger number of
reports, resulting in improved processing efficiency.
The observed performance trend aligns with the principles of

In the context of Griffin Model 1.0, semantic analysis, curriculum mapping, and report evaluation

efficiency compared to isolated report evaluation.
The results suggest that Griffin Model 1.0 is well-suited for institutional deployment scenarios
involving large numbers of internship reports, project reports, and academic submissions. The
ability to perform bulk assessment with decreasing average processing time highlights the
framework's potential for supporting large-scale academic evaluation while reducing faculty
workload and improving assessment throughput.

tokens.heading: 4.9 Discussion
tokens.text:
The experimental findings demonstrate that Griffin Model 1.0 successfully performs curriculum-
aware internship report assessment through the integration of semantic analysis, curriculum
mapping, and significance evaluation. The framework effectively identifies curriculum coverage,
evaluates educational relevance, and generates interpretable assessment outcomes.
Unlike conventional assessment approaches that primarily focus on content quality or textual
similarity, the proposed framework evaluates both educational alignment and technical
contribution. The observed results indicate that curriculum-aware assessment can improve
evaluation consistency while reducing manual effort required during academic assessment
processes.
